translations.literal: Once the Last Emperor was enthroned, Yan believed he had great merit toward Liang and had also married a princess; hearing that Tang’s imperial son-in-law Du Cong had risen to general and minister and lived in great splendor, he was shamed that he did not match him.
translations.idiomatic: Enthroned, Yan counted his service to Liang and his princess marriage high. Tang’s son-in-law Du Cong had reached general and minister and lived in splendor—Yan burned with shame that he had not.

sentences.zh: 乃占天下良田大宅，裒刻商旅，其門如市，租庸之物，半入其私，巖飲食必費萬錢。

translations.literal: He then seized the empire’s best fields and great houses, extorted merchants, and his gate was like a market; half the transport-tax goods went into his private purse, and a single meal cost him ten thousand cash.
translations.idiomatic: He seized the best land and mansions in the realm, shook down merchants until his gate thronged like a market, skimmed half the transport tax into his pocket, and spent ten thousand cash on a single meal.

sentences.zh: 故時，魏州牙兵驕，數為亂，羅紹威盡誅之。

translations.literal: In former times the Wei Prefecture guard troops had been insolent and often rebelled; Luo Shaowei killed them all.
translations.idiomatic: Wei’s guard troops had once been proud and mutinous; Luo Shaowei slaughtered them to the last man.

sentences.zh: 太祖崩，楊師厚逐羅氏，據魏州，復置牙兵二千，末帝患之。

translations.literal: When the Founder died, Yang Shihou drove out the Luo clan, seized Wei Prefecture, and re-established two thousand guard troops; the Last Emperor was troubled by it.
translations.idiomatic: At the Founder’s death Yang Shihou expelled the Luo house, took Wei, and raised two thousand guard troops again. The Last Emperor brooded over it.

sentences.zh: 師厚死，巖與租庸判官邵贊議曰：「魏為唐患，百有餘年，自先帝時，嘗切齒紹威，以其前恭而後倨。

translations.literal: When Shihou died, Yan and transport-tax judge Shao Zan deliberated, saying: “Wei has been Tang’s affliction for more than a hundred years. Even in the Founder’s time he gnashed his teeth at Shaowei for first bowing and later turning proud.
translations.idiomatic: After Shihou died, Yan and tax judge Shao Zan argued: “Wei has plagued Tang for a century. The Founder himself gnashed his teeth at Shaowei—humble at first, arrogant later.

sentences.zh: 今先帝新棄天下，師厚復為陛下憂，所以然者，以魏地大而兵多也。

translations.literal: Now the Founder has only just left the world, and Shihou again troubles Your Majesty—all because Wei’s territory is large and its soldiers many.
translations.idiomatic: The Founder is barely in his grave and Shihou’s shadow already haunts you—because Wei is vast and its armies numerous.

sentences.zh: 陛下不以此時制之，寧知後人不為師厚也？

translations.literal: If Your Majesty does not curb it now, who knows whether those who come after will not be another Shihou?
translations.idiomatic: If you do not break it now, the next man may be another Shihou.

sentences.zh: 不若分相、魏為兩鎮，則無北顧之憂矣。

translations.literal: Better to split Xiang and Wei into two circuits—then there will be no worry over the north.
translations.idiomatic: Split Xiang and Wei into two commands, and the north need never trouble you again.

sentences.zh: 」末帝以為然，乃分相、澶、衛為昭德軍。

translations.literal: ” The Last Emperor thought it right and thereupon split Xiang, Cang, and Wei into the Zhaode army.
translations.idiomatic: ” The Last Emperor agreed and carved Xiang, Cang, and Wei into the Zhaode command.

sentences.zh: 牙兵亂，以魏博降晉，梁由是盡失河北。

translations.literal: The guard troops mutinied; Wei-Bo submitted to Jin, and Liang thereby lost all of Hebei.
translations.idiomatic: The guard troops rose. Wei-Bo went over to Jin, and Liang lost Hebei entire.

sentences.zh: 鎮州張文禮殺王镕，使人告梁曰：「臣已北召契丹，願梁以兵萬人出德、棣州，則晉兵憊矣。

translations.literal: Zhang Wenli of Zhen Prefecture killed Wang Rong and sent word to Liang: “Your servant has already summoned Khitan from the north; if Liang will march ten thousand men out of De and Di prefectures, the Jin army will be exhausted.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Wenli of Zhen murdered Wang Rong and wrote Liang: “I have called Khitan from the north. Send ten thousand men from De and Di, and Jin will break.

sentences.zh: 」敬翔以為然，巖與漢傑皆以為不可，乃止。

translations.literal: ” Jing Xiang thought it right, but Yan and Hanjie both said it could not be done, and so it stopped.
translations.idiomatic: ” Jing Xiang agreed; Yan and Hanjie refused, and nothing was done.

sentences.zh: 其後黜王彥章用段凝，皆巖力也。

translations.literal: Later the dismissal of Wang Yanzhang and the use of Duan Ning were both Yan’s doing.
translations.idiomatic: Later the fall of Wang Yanzhang and the rise of Duan Ning were Yan’s work.

sentences.zh: 莊宗兵將至汴，末帝惶惑不知所為，登建國樓以問群臣，或曰：「晉以孤軍遠來，勢難持久，雖使入汴，不能守也。

translations.literal: When Zhuangzong’s army was about to reach Bian, the Last Emperor was fearful and did not know what to do. He ascended the Jianguo Tower to ask his ministers. Some said: “Jin comes with a lone army from afar; the situation is hard to sustain. Even if they enter Bian they cannot hold it.
translations.idiomatic: As Zhuangzong neared Bian the Last Emperor panicked. On the Jianguo Tower he asked his ministers. Some said: “Jin marches far with a thin host. Even if they enter Bian they cannot keep it.

sentences.zh: 宜幸洛陽，保險以召天下兵，徐圖之，勝負未可知也。

translations.literal: Your Majesty should go to Luoyang, hold the defiles, summon the empire’s armies, and plan slowly—the outcome is not yet known.
translations.idiomatic: Flee to Luoyang, hold the passes, rally the realm’s armies, and wait—the fight is not lost.

sentences.zh: 」末帝猶豫，巖曰：「勢已如此，一下此樓，何人可保！

translations.literal: ” The Last Emperor hesitated. Yan said: “The situation is already thus—once you descend this tower, who can guarantee you?
translations.idiomatic: ” He wavered. Yan said: “It has come to this. Step off this tower and who will answer for your life?

sentences.zh: 」末帝卒死於樓上。

translations.literal: ” The Last Emperor in the end died on the tower.
translations.idiomatic: ” In the end he died on the tower.

sentences.zh: 當巖用事時，許州溫韜尤曲事巖，巖因顧其左右曰：「吾常待韜厚，今以急投之，必不幸吾為利。

translations.literal: While Yan held power, Xu Prefecture’s Wen Tao fawned on him above all. Yan therefore said to his attendants: “I have always treated Tao generously; now I run to him in peril—he will surely not betray me for profit.
translations.idiomatic: In Yan’s days Xu’s Wen Tao flattered him hardest. Yan told his men: “I have been good to Tao. Now I flee to him—he will not sell me.

sentences.zh: 」乃走投韜，韜斬其首以獻。

translations.literal: ” He then fled to seek Tao; Tao cut off his head and presented it.
translations.idiomatic: ” He ran to Tao. Tao took his head and sent it in.

sentences.zh: 莊宗已滅梁，巖素所善段凝奏請誅巖家屬，乃族滅之。

translations.literal: After Zhuangzong had destroyed Liang, Duan Ning—whom Yan had favored—memorialized that Yan’s kin be executed, and the clan was exterminated to the last.
translations.idiomatic: Liang fell. Duan Ning, whom Yan had favored, asked that Yan’s house be wiped out—and it was.

sentences.zh: 嗚呼，禍福之理，豈可一哉！

translations.literal: Alas—the principle of fortune and calamity, can it be one thing only?
translations.idiomatic: Alas—can fortune and ruin ever be one simple thing?

sentences.zh: 君子小人之禍福異也。

translations.literal: The fortune and calamity of the gentleman and the petty man differ.
translations.idiomatic: Gentlemen and petty men do not meet the same fate.

sentences.zh: 老子曰：「禍兮福所倚，福兮禍所伏。

translations.literal: Laozi said: “Calamity—upon it fortune leans; fortune—within it calamity hides.
translations.idiomatic: Laozi said: “Calamity is where fortune leans; fortune is where calamity hides.

sentences.zh: 」後世之談禍福者，皆以其言為至論也。

translations.literal: ” Later talkers on fortune and calamity have all taken his words as the last word.
translations.idiomatic: ” Later moralizers have treated that as the final truth about luck.

sentences.zh: 夫為善而受福，焉得禍？

translations.literal: Do good and receive fortune—how then calamity?
translations.idiomatic: Do good and win blessing—where is the ruin in that?

sentences.zh: 為惡而受禍，焉得福？

translations.literal: Do evil and receive calamity—how then fortune?
translations.idiomatic: Do evil and earn disaster—where is the luck in that?

sentences.zh: 惟君子之罹非禍者，未必不為福；

translations.literal: Only when the gentleman suffers what is not fortune, it may yet prove fortune;
translations.idiomatic: Only the gentleman who suffers what looks like ill luck may yet find luck in it;

sentences.zh: 小人求非福者，未嘗不及禍，此自然之理也。

translations.literal: the petty man who seeks what is not calamity has never failed to meet calamity—this is the natural principle.
translations.idiomatic: the petty man who chases what looks like luck has never missed ruin. That is nature’s law.

sentences.zh: 始，犨自以先見之明，深結梁太祖，及其子孫皆享其祿利，自謂知所托矣，安知其族卒與梁俱滅也？

translations.literal: At first Chou, trusting his foresight, bound himself deeply to Liang Taizu, and his sons and grandsons all enjoyed its salaries and profits, believing he knew whom to rely on—who knew his clan would in the end perish with Liang?
translations.idiomatic: Chou trusted his foresight, clung to Taizu, and saw his sons and grandsons feast on Liang’s favor, sure he had chosen well—who dreamed the house would die with Liang?

sentences.zh: 犨之求福於梁，蓋老氏之所謂福也，非君子之所求也，不可戒哉！

translations.literal: Chou’s seeking fortune from Liang was the fortune Laozi speaks of—not what the gentleman seeks. Let it be a warning!
translations.idiomatic: The fortune Chou sought from Liang was Laozi’s kind of fortune, not the gentleman’s. Take warning.

sentences.zh: 馮行襲

translations.literal: Feng Xingxi
translations.idiomatic: Feng Xingxi

sentences.zh: 馮行襲，字正臣，均州人也。

translations.literal: Feng Xingxi, styled Zhengchen, was a native of Jun Prefecture.
translations.idiomatic: Feng Xingxi, styled Zhengchen, came from Jun Prefecture.

sentences.zh: 唐末，山南盜孫喜以眾千人襲均州刺史呂燁，燁不能禦。

translations.literal: At the end of Tang, the Shannan bandit Sun Xi with a force of a thousand men attacked Jun Prefecture’s prefect Lü Ye; Ye could not resist.
translations.idiomatic: Late in Tang the Shannan outlaw Sun Xi struck Jun with a thousand men. Prefect Lü Ye could not hold him.

sentences.zh: 行襲為州校，乃陰選勇士伏江南，獨乘小舟逆喜，告曰：「州人聞公至，皆欲歸矣。

translations.literal: Xingxi was a prefectural soldier; he secretly chose brave men and hid them south of the river, then alone took a small boat upstream to meet Xi and said: “The people of the prefecture, hearing you have come, all wish to submit.
translations.idiomatic: Xingxi was a prefectural trooper. He hid picked men south of the river, took a skiff alone upstream to Xi, and said: “Jun’s people hear you are coming and wish to yield.

sentences.zh: 然知公兵多，民懼虜掠，恐其驚擾，請留兵江北，獨與腹心數人從行，願為前導，以慰安州民，事可立定。

translations.literal: Yet knowing your soldiers are many, the people fear plunder and disturbance; lest they panic, please leave your troops on the north bank of the river and come with only a few trusted men in your train—I will guide you ahead to reassure the people of the prefecture, and the matter can be settled at once.
translations.idiomatic: But your host is large and they fear looting. Leave your men on the north bank; cross with only your inner circle. I will go ahead to calm the town, and all will be settled quickly.

sentences.zh: 」喜以為然，乃留其兵江北，獨與行襲渡江。

translations.literal: ” Xi thought it right and thereupon left his troops on the north bank and crossed the river with Xingxi alone.
translations.idiomatic: ” Xi agreed, left his army north of the river, and crossed with Xingxi alone.

sentences.zh: 軍吏前謁，行襲擊喜仆地，斬之，伏兵發，盡殺從行者。

translations.literal: Army clerks came forward to pay respects; Xingxi struck Xi to the ground, beheaded him, the hidden troops sprang forth, and all who had followed were killed.
translations.idiomatic: Clerks came to greet them. Xingxi knocked Xi down and took his head; the ambush rose and killed every man who had crossed.

sentences.zh: 餘兵在江北，聞喜死，皆潰。

translations.literal: The remaining troops on the north bank, hearing Xi was dead, all scattered.
translations.idiomatic: North of the river the rest heard Xi was dead and melted away.

sentences.zh: 山南節度使劉巨容表行襲均州刺史。

translations.literal: The Shannan military commissioner Liu Jurong memorialized Xingxi as prefect of Jun.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Jurong of Shannan made him prefect of Jun.

sentences.zh: 是時，僖宗在蜀，諸鎮貢獻行在者皆道山南，盜賊多據州西長山以邀劫之，行襲盡破諸賊。

translations.literal: At that time Zhaozong was in Shu; the circuits that sent tribute to the mobile court all passed through Shannan, and bandits often held Changshan west of the prefecture to waylay them—Xingxi broke every such band.
translations.idiomatic: Zhaozong was in Shu; tribute routes ran through Shannan, and robbers held Changshan west of the prefecture to ambush them. Xingxi broke band after band.

sentences.zh: 洋州葛佐辟行襲行軍司馬，使以兵鎮谷口，通秦、蜀道，行襲由此知名。

translations.literal: Yang Prefecture’s Ge Zuo recruited Xingxi as acting army marshal and sent him with troops to hold Gukou and keep open the Qin-Shu road; Xingxi became famous from this.
translations.idiomatic: Ge Zuo of Yang Prefecture took him as acting army marshal, posted him at Gukou to hold the Qin-Shu road open, and his name spread.

sentences.zh: 李茂貞兼領山南，遣子繼臻守金州，行襲逐之，遂據金州。

translations.literal: Li Maozhen also held Shannan and sent his son Jizhen to guard Jin Prefecture; Xingxi drove him out and thereupon seized Jin.
translations.idiomatic: Li Maozhen held Shannan too and sent his son Jizhen to guard Jin. Xingxi expelled him and took Jin.

sentences.zh: 昭宗乃以金州為戎昭軍，拜行襲節度使。

translations.literal: Zhaozong then made Jin the Rongzhao army and appointed Xingxi its military commissioner.
translations.idiomatic: Zhaozong formed the Rongzhao command at Jin and made Xingxi its commissioner.

sentences.zh: 昭宗在岐，梁太祖引兵而西，中尉韓全誨遣中官郤文晏等二十餘人召兵江淮，以拒太祖，行襲已附梁，乃盡殺文晏等。

translations.literal: When Zhaozong was at Qi, Liang Taizu led troops west; the inner palace attendant Han Quanhui sent more than twenty eunuchs such as Xi Wenyan to summon troops from the Jiang-Huai to resist Taizu. Xingxi had already submitted to Liang and thereupon killed Wenyan and the rest.
translations.idiomatic: Zhaozong was at Qi when Taizu marched west. Han Quanhui sent twenty-odd eunuchs including Xi Wenyan to raise Jiang-Huai troops against him. Xingxi had already bowed to Liang and killed them all.

sentences.zh: 太祖攻趙匡凝於襄陽，行襲遣子勖以舟兵會均、房，以功遷匡國軍節度使。

translations.literal: When Taizu attacked Zhao Kuangning at Xiangyang, Xingxi sent his son Xu with river troops from Jun and Fang to join him; for this merit he was transferred to military commissioner of the Kuangguo army.
translations.idiomatic: Taizu besieged Zhao Kuangning at Xiangyang. Xingxi sent his son Xu with river forces from Jun and Fang. For that service he was made Kuangguo military commissioner.

sentences.zh: 行襲為人嚴酷少恩，而所至輒天幸，境旱有蝗，則飛鳥食之，歲兇，田中鹵谷自生。

translations.literal: Xingxi as a man was harsh and sparing of kindness, yet wherever he went fortune seemed to follow: if locusts plagued the land, birds ate them; if the year failed, salty grain sprang up in the fields by itself.
translations.idiomatic: He was harsh and stingy with mercy, yet luck dogged him: locusts came and birds devoured them; famine years and salty grain sprang from the fields on its own.

sentences.zh: 唐衰，知梁必興，尤盡心傾附事梁，官至司空，封長樂郡王，卒贈太傅，謚曰忠敬。

translations.literal: When Tang declined, knowing Liang would surely rise, he especially devoted his heart in wholehearted attachment and served Liang; he rose to Minister of Works, was enfeoffed as Prince of Changle commandery, and upon death was posthumously granted Grand Preceptor with the posthumous title Loyal and Reverent.
translations.idiomatic: As Tang waned he saw Liang rising and gave it his whole loyalty; he rose to Minister of Works and was made Prince of Changle, and when he died was posthumously honored as Grand Preceptor with the epithet Loyal and Reverent.
